Work out the amount in several labeled example servings.
Multiply the value per serving by the number of servings. These are example labels, not dietary targets.
Pair each example portion with its matching panel.
Portion and panel have to agree. A bigger portion changes the amount, not the food.
Recover a missing number from a whole-recipe total.
The stated example total equals the sum of all the parts.
Balance two plates by changing their portion counts.
Equal quantities can be written as different numbers of servings.
Find the claim the displayed example label actually supports.
A panel supports the numbers it states. It does not establish a health outcome or allergen safety.
Find the interval that rounds to the displayed number.
This uses ordinary mathematical rounding to the nearest ten; it is not a simulation of FDA labeling rules.
Arrange example ingredients from most to least by mass.
Compare the displayed gram amounts, not the size of the ingredient name.
Choose three ingredients that meet the plate's category rules.
The rules are a neutral construction puzzle, not a prescription for a balanced diet.
Combine fictional portions to reach an exact example total.
Add the displayed example grams. This target is a puzzle, not a personal protein recommendation.
Find every example order inside the requested range.
Both ends of the requested range count. Smaller numbers do not earn extra points.
Collect marked tokens along a path to the exit.
Each token is explicitly labeled with fictional fiber grams. The goal is route planning, not dietary advice.
Sort equal-sized example servings by sodium.
Compare milligrams for the same serving definition. These fictional values teach units and ordering.
Reconstruct a real tracked restaurant order from its included items.
Only the listed order is supported. Extra selections are not verified customizations. U.S. menu data; portions and source are shown.
Find the orders that satisfy two displayed priorities together.
A match must satisfy both stated numerical rules; one favorable value does not cancel the other.
Move the basket beneath the requested fruit before dropping it.
Use left and right, then Catch. Untimed turns make this playable without fast reactions.
Guide the carrot through a small garden maze.
Move one square at a time. Walls stay fixed; reaching the gate finishes the route.
Pick up picnic parcels, then bring them to the table.
Visit each parcel before the table. You can plan the route at your own pace.
Return the berry with the paddle until the targets are cleared.
Choose the paddle lane, then advance the bounce. Predict the ball's next lane; no timer is required.
Repeat the displayed beat pattern in its correct order.
Each beat is a visual cue. Sound is off and there is no reaction-time penalty.
Turn the orbit and land at the marked platform.
Advance the orange around the ring, then land when its numbered position matches the target.
Stack beans while keeping their combined center over the base.
The average position of the stack must stay within the marked support. This is simplified fictional physics.
Fit every pantry piece into the available grid.
Pieces cannot overlap or leave the grid. Choose a piece, rotate it, and place its top-left square.
Follow the preparation steps in order through the grid.
The numbered steps must be visited in sequence before the finish square.
Rotate the pipes into a connected water route.
Each connected pair must share an open edge. The water needs a continuous path from start to finish.
Slide the illustrated tiles back into order.
Only a tile beside the empty square can move. The puzzle is shuffled by legal moves so it is solvable.
Fill the orchard pattern using row and column clues.
Each clue lists lengths of consecutive filled runs. Separate runs with at least one empty square.
Cover a diamond-shaped lunch silhouette with four geometric pieces.
The pieces cover the marked silhouette exactly, without overlapping or entering unmarked cells. This is an original grid mosaic rather than a traditional seven-piece tangram.
Place four picnic items into compartments using position clues.
Each compartment holds one item. All the displayed clues must be true together.
Put the shuffled letters back into an ingredient name.
Every letter is used once. Duplicate letters are separate tiles.
Complete a small intersecting food crossword.
Both answers must satisfy their clues and agree at the shared letter.
Find three food words hidden in the letter grid.
Select the first and last letter. Words run horizontally, vertically or diagonally, forward only.
Sort eight kitchen words into two precise groups.
Select four words sharing one stated connection, then find the other group. No obscure trick categories.
Pair ingredient descriptions with the right names.
Use the specific shape and preparation descriptions. These clues are not health claims.
Connect three terms to their exact explanations.
Serving size is the label's reference amount; total carbohydrate and protein are nutrient quantities. Terms are educational, not personal guidance.
Choose the excerpt that supports the claim without overreaching.
Evidence should state the quantity, population or scope actually claimed. A plausible headline is not enough.
Find all four pairs of original food characters.
Reveal two tiles at a time. A mismatch remains visible until you choose Continue, so nobody has to race a timer.
Find the three swapped items between two picnic scenes.
Compare each matching position. Only three positions contain a different item.
Study an order, then rebuild its sequence from memory.
Hide the order when ready. You can study it again without penalty.
Study the pantry and recall how many requested items it held.
The whole pantry remains visible until you choose to hide it. Use Study again whenever needed.
Repeat a growing sequence of food characters.
Complete lengths two, three and four. Study the sequence at your own pace before each round.
Recognize an ingredient from its original silhouette.
Compare shape, not color. The full food character is revealed after a correct answer.
Find the item that does not satisfy the stated shape rule.
The rule is printed explicitly so the answer never depends on an ambiguous food classification.
Arrange food stamps into your own plate and save the result.
There is no best plate and no nutrition score. Place at least three stamps; your artwork stays on this device.
Mix colored fictional ingredients to match a recipe's ratio.
This is a color-and-ratio puzzle, not a nutrition calculator. Each scoop is an equal-sized fictional part.
Rebuild the requested sandwich from bottom to top.
The layer order matters. Repeated bread layers use separate tiles.
Give an original ingredient character its own expression.
Choose a body, eyes and expression, then save your character locally. No name or personal information is requested.
Replace missing example ingredients while preserving recipe roles.
These are fictional recipe roles, not guaranteed real-world substitutions or allergen-safe suggestions.
Fill a fictional market basket within a budget and item count.
Prices are invented puzzle tokens, not current restaurant or grocery prices.
Pack a picnic kit with enough seats and drinks within its space limit.
Capacity and planning numbers are fictional. This puzzle is about allocating space, not limiting food intake.
Identify a tracked U.S. order from progressively revealed clues.
Clues come from the stored verified values. Unknown values are never treated as zero; source and serving are shown after solving.
Complete the missing cells so all row and column totals agree.
These are invented gram totals. Add across rows and down columns; this is not a daily macro plan.
Shade equivalent fractions of two differently divided plates.
Equal fractions can have different denominators. Both plate fractions must match the requested amount.
Visit fictional restaurants on a map with a short closed route.
The map, distances and delivery scenario are fictional. Distance is measured in grid units.
Route the next item into the requested destination as belts change.
Read the current routing table before each dispatch. The same switch can lead somewhere different on the next turn.
Order three processing switches to produce the requested symbol string.
Operations transform symbols, not real food chemistry. Order changes the output.
Join all the ingredient tiles by their matching edge tags.
Tiles can turn around. The next tile's left tag must equal the previous tile's right tag.
